title: Ser and estar, the hard part
description: Say what something is, and how it is.
grammarNote: Ser says what something is. Estar says how it is, where it is, or how it is going.

explanation.summary: By now ser and estar are familiar. The advanced part is knowing which one a particular meaning needs, and knowing the fixed phrases where Spanish does not follow the rule you would expect.

sections.heading: The three jobs of estar
sections.body: Estar is for where a thing is, how a thing is right now, and how a thing is going. Ser is for what a thing is, who a thing is, and what it is made of. The tricky part is that some words change meaning with the verb: un café es frío, coffee is a cold thing, and el café está frío, the coffee has gone cold.

examples.es: La reunión es a las nueve.
La reunión está a las nueve.
examples.en: The meeting is running at nine.
examples.note: A meeting in progress uses estar.

sections.heading: The fixed phrases
sections.body: Some expressions take one verb in Spanish and the other in English. Ser rico is to be rich, but estar rico means to be delicious. Estar listo means to be ready, but ser listo means to be clever. And estar bien means to be well, while ser bueno means to be a good person.

examples.note: Estar rico is about the food.
Ser rico is about the price.
Estar listo is to be ready.

items.note: It goes with estar: el proyecto está en marcha.
A point of the infinitive: está a punto de salir.
De acuerdo con: de acuerdo con el plan.
It agrees with what was just said.
A phrase that softens a statement: en realidad, no es tan difícil.
It sums up what has been said.
Por ahora no sé, I do not know for now.
